claims.text: Near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles can be synthesized as a single solid-solution phase with an initially homogeneous elemental distribution.
An optimal balance of mixing enthalpy can be achieved by tuning elemental ratios such as Co/Mo.
High configurational entropy can overcome the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation when mixing enthalpy is optimally balanced.
This enthalpy-entropy balance enhances preservation of a single-phase structure under high-temperature catalytic conditions.
The Co/Mo ratio in quinary CoMoFeNiCu nanoparticles can be systematically controlled.
Changing Co/Mo ratio while holding all other synthesis parameters constant selectively modulates mixing enthalpy.
Phase-diagram-inspired parameters can provide information relevant to solid-solution phase stability.
An effective mixing enthalpy can be derived from phase-diagram-inspired parameters.
Effective mixing enthalpy mediates atomic diffusion kinetics during high-temperature exposure.
Effective mixing enthalpy suppresses phase separation during high-temperature exposure.
An optimal mixing enthalpy allows configurational entropy to dominate the alloy's stability.
Configurational-entropy dominance reduces the thermodynamic driving force for phase segregation.
The proposed thermodynamic balance limits atomic diffusion that would otherwise cause structural degradation.
Nanoparticles with optimized mixing enthalpy will retain a single-phase solid solution during prolonged exposure at 773–1173 K better than the baseline.
Nanoparticles with optimized mixing enthalpy will maintain catalytic performance during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Compositions outside the optimal mixing-enthalpy window will undergo significant phase separation and lose catalytic activity.
Standard near-equiatomic nanoparticles exhibit measurable structural degradation or phase separation under the proposed high-temperature conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies over 773–1173 K but may fail outside that range or when rapid oxidation dominates degradation.
The optimal mixing-enthalpy window and its relationship to diffusion barriers are not quantitatively established by direct long-term measurements.

Failure of the tuned samples to show statistically significant improvements in structural stability and catalytic activity over the baseline would falsify the proposed primary role of mixing enthalpy.
